title: How Much Money Can You Send from UK to India?
excerpt: Understand why UK-to-India transfer limits vary by provider and payment route, and prepare for identity, source-of-funds and recipient checks.

blocks.html: The short answer

There is no single number that answers how much money can you send from UK to India in every situation. Your practical limit can depend on the transfer provider, the way you fund the payment, the Indian payout route, the purpose of the transfer and the checks required for that transaction.

A provider may publish a per-transfer, daily or account limit. Your UK bank can apply its own online-payment limit. An Indian remittance route may also have separate conditions. A limit shown in an app is therefore not necessarily a universal UK or Indian legal ceiling.

Large legitimate transfers are possible through suitable regulated routes, but they commonly receive more scrutiny. Be ready to explain where the money came from, why it is being sent and who will receive it. Approval is never guaranteed merely because the amount sits below a displayed limit.

This guide provides general information, not legal, tax or financial advice. For a property purchase, business payment, investment, inheritance or other high-value transaction, confirm the route with the provider, receiving bank and an appropriately qualified adviser.
Why limits differ

The word "limit" can describe several different things. A provider limit is the maximum its system accepts. A bank limit controls how much you can send from your account. A payout-scheme limit belongs to the route used in India. A compliance review is not a published limit at all, but it can pause a transfer while evidence is checked.

These layers can overlap. Suppose a provider allows a large international transfer but your UK bank permits a smaller online payment. You may need to arrange a bank transfer through a different channel. That does not mean dividing the transaction into artificial pieces to avoid checks.

The receiving bank may ask about the purpose or beneficiary. A family-maintenance payment is not the same as a property payment, investment or commercial invoice. Selecting an inaccurate purpose simply to make a transfer go through can create delays and record-keeping problems.

Ask a precise question: "What is the maximum for this funding method, recipient account, payout route and transfer purpose?" That is more useful than asking only for the provider's largest advertised number.
The transfer route
India has more than one route for receiving money from abroad. A bank-to-bank transfer and a cash-oriented personal-remittance service do not necessarily use the same framework.

The Reserve Bank of India explains that its Money Transfer Service Scheme, or MTSS, is for inward personal remittances such as family maintenance and remittances for foreign tourists. Its published FAQ describes an individual remittance cap and an annual count for that particular scheme. It also says certain purposes, including property purchases, investments and credits to NRE accounts, are not allowed through MTSS.

Those MTSS conditions should not be copied across to every bank deposit. The RBI's inward-remittance FAQ distinguishes MTSS from other arrangements. A large account-to-account remittance may use a different banking route with different conditions.
This distinction explains why two apparently conflicting limit figures can both be genuine. They may describe different services. Before relying on a number, identify the route to which it belongs.
Provider limits

Transfer companies set operational and risk limits based on account verification, currency, payment method and destination. A new or partially verified account may have a lower usable limit than a fully reviewed account.

Some providers display the maximum after you enter the currencies and funding method. Others ask customers to contact a specialist team for large payments. Published limits can change, so check the provider's current terms rather than relying on an old comparison article or screenshot.

Also distinguish the sending limit from the guaranteed conversion amount. The exchange rate may remain available only for a stated period. If your bank payment or compliance review arrives late, the quote may expire even though the transfer itself remains within the provider's limit.
The UK-to-India transfer-fees guide helps you compare the final INR amount rather than treating a large limit as proof of good value.
Your UK bank

Your bank may restrict online, mobile or telephone payments. The figure can differ by channel and can be lower for a new payee. Fraud-prevention checks may hold an unusual or high-value payment while the bank confirms that you authorised it.

Ask whether the cap is per transaction or per day, and whether it applies to Faster Payments, CHAPS, card funding or an international transfer. Also ask about charges. A higher-limit route can carry a different fee.

Do not assume that a declined payment means the transfer provider rejected you. The sending bank, card issuer and provider are separate parties. The error message or support team should identify which stage stopped the payment.

For a direct bank route, use the checklist in the bank transfer from UK to India guide. If the payment is travelling through correspondent banks, the SWIFT transfer guide explains the additional details and possible deductions.
Verification checks

A provider must understand its customer and monitor transactions. The amount is only one factor. A payment can be reviewed because it differs from normal account activity, has an unclear purpose, involves inconsistent names or needs additional source-of-funds evidence.

For a substantial transfer, prepare the evidence before a deadline becomes urgent. Depending on the source, that might include recent bank records, salary evidence, a completion statement, probate records, investment-sale evidence or business documents.

The evidence should form a coherent trail. A bank statement showing a balance may not explain how the balance arose. If money moved between your own accounts, keep records that connect the original source to the account used for funding.
Read the transfer documents guide for a practical preparation list. Upload only what the provider requests through its official secure channel.
Recipient details

A large transfer is more likely to fail when recipient details are incomplete or inconsistent. Confirm the beneficiary's full account name, account number, IFSC code, bank and branch details. For a SWIFT route, verify any requested BIC or intermediary information.

Check whether the recipient account can accept the stated purpose and currency. If you are sending to your own NRE account, use a route that supports that credit. The NRE account transfer guide explains the practical distinction.

Do not reuse old details without asking the recipient to confirm them. Bank mergers, branch changes and account restrictions can affect a transfer. Independently verify any last-minute change received by email or messaging app because changed payment details are a common fraud warning.
Purpose matters
The amount alone does not decide whether a transfer is appropriate. The reason for the payment affects the route, documents and possible tax treatment.

Family support, your own savings, a gift, tuition, property, an investment and payment for services are different purposes. A provider may request an invoice, admission record, sale agreement, gift explanation or proof of relationship.

Do not label a commercial payment as family maintenance. Do not label a loan as a gift. A truthful description protects the records of both sender and recipient and helps the receiving bank apply the correct reporting category.

If the money is related to a property transaction, company, trust or estate, obtain specialist guidance before sending. The transfer provider processes money; it does not necessarily decide your legal or tax position.
Transfer tax
A transfer limit and a tax rule answer different questions. Moving money does not automatically make it taxable, but the underlying receipt or transaction may have tax consequences.

For example, money returned to your own account is different from salary, business income, sale proceeds, a loan or a gift. A gift from a defined relative may be treated differently from money received from another person under Indian tax rules.
Keep evidence of the source, purpose and relationship. The separate UK-to-India transfer tax guide explains the main questions without treating every remittance as income.

For a significant payment, ask an Indian tax professional about the recipient's circumstances and a UK adviser about any issue connected with the sender or source. A provider saying "transfer permitted" is not a tax ruling.
A worked plan
Imagine you want to send GBP 60,000 from your UK savings to your own eligible Indian account. The figure is illustrative, not a statement of any provider's current limit.

First, confirm that the provider supports the account type and purpose. Second, check its current per-transfer and account limits. Third, check your bank's funding limit and charge. Fourth, prepare statements showing how the savings accumulated. Fifth, verify the beneficiary details through a trusted channel.
Next, compare the provider's final INR payout with the live reference calculation. The pound to INR converter supplies a benchmark, not a guaranteed transaction rate.
Finally, allow time for review and banking stages. The transfer-time guide explains why a provider estimate is not an unconditional arrival promise.
Avoid splitting

Do not divide a large transfer into smaller payments for the purpose of avoiding verification or reporting checks. Related transactions can be considered together, and artificial splitting may create more questions rather than fewer.
There are legitimate reasons to send in stages, such as contract milestones or rate-risk management. Document that reason and ask the provider how repeated payments affect limits and fees.
Multiple small transfers can also cost more if each carries a fixed fee. Compare the total recipient amount across the complete plan, not the attractive appearance of one small quote.
Before sending
Confirm the exact route, current provider limit, funding limit and recipient-account eligibility. Check the purpose description and gather source-of-funds evidence.

Compare the exchange-rate margin, visible fees and possible receiving deductions. Read the quote-expiry terms and cancellation process. Verify recipient details independently, especially after any unexpected change.
Keep the quote, transfer reference, funding confirmation and recipient receipt. These records can help with tracing, tax questions or a later refund.
Common questions
Is there one UK legal limit for sending money to India?
There is no single practical number that covers every provider and route. Current provider, bank, payout-scheme and compliance conditions must be checked for the specific transfer.
Can I send a very large amount in one transfer?
Possibly, through a suitable route and provider. Expect additional evidence and confirm the receiving purpose and account before funding it.
Does a transfer below the provider limit avoid checks?
No. Checks can depend on risk, account activity, identity, source, recipient and purpose as well as amount.
Should I split a transfer to stay below a limit?
Do not split payments to avoid controls. If staged payments have a genuine commercial or practical reason, document it and ask how the provider handles them.
Is the maximum amount also the cheapest amount to send?
No. Limits and value are separate. Compare the complete INR payout, fees, exchange-rate margin, speed and route for the amount you actually need to send.

title: Is Money Sent from UK to India Taxable?
excerpt: Understand why tax depends on the purpose and recipient of a UK-to-India transfer, with practical guidance for gifts, support and own-account payments.

blocks.html: The short answer

If you are asking is money sent from UK to India taxable, the bank transfer itself is not enough to decide. Tax treatment depends on what the money represents, who owns it, why it is being paid, the relationship between sender and recipient and the tax residence of the people involved.

Moving your existing savings to another account in your own name is different from paying salary, buying property, giving money to a relative or sending a gift to someone who is not a defined relative. The receiving bank description does not change the true nature of the transaction.

Many genuine family-support transfers are not taxed merely because they arrive from the UK. However, that does not mean every overseas credit is automatically tax-free. Income can remain income, and Indian gift rules can apply to money received without consideration.

This guide explains the questions to ask and the records to keep. It is general education, not tax advice. For a large gift, property payment, business receipt, estate distribution or unusual residence position, obtain advice based on the full facts.
Start with purpose
The first question is not the exchange rate or the provider. Ask: what does the money actually represent?

Common answers include your own savings, family maintenance, a personal gift, repayment of a loan, salary, payment for freelance work, rent, sale proceeds, inheritance, an investment or a property purchase. Each answer can lead to a different analysis.

A provider may ask you to select a purpose from a menu. Choose the accurate purpose and keep evidence that supports it. Describing income as a gift does not make it a gift. Calling a gift family maintenance does not remove any record-keeping or tax question.

For a high-value payment, write a simple note before sending: sender, recipient, relationship, source of money, purpose and whether repayment is expected. This makes later questions easier to answer consistently.
Your own account

Sending money from your UK account to an Indian account that you also own is generally a movement of your funds, not automatically new income created by the transfer. But the source and destination still matter.

If the money came from taxable salary, a business, rent, investments or an asset sale, any tax issue connected with that source does not disappear when the funds move. The transfer itself and the event that produced the money are separate.

Account type matters too. NRE and NRO accounts are designed for different kinds of funds and have different operating and repatriation considerations. The NRE versus NRO guide gives a practical overview, while the NRE transfer guide explains the sending steps.

Keep both sides of the trail: the UK debit, provider confirmation, conversion details and Indian credit. If the transfer is between accounts in your own name, matching names and clear statements can help demonstrate that fact.
Family support

People commonly send money from the UK to parents, a spouse or other family members in India for living costs, healthcare or education. The fact that a payment is family support does not by itself provide a complete tax answer, but the relationship is important.
Indian income-tax rules provide exceptions for gifts received from specified relatives. The statutory definition matters; everyday use of the word "relative" can be broader than the tax definition.
For example, a close family relationship that feels obvious socially should still be checked against the defined list. Do not assume that every cousin, family friend or extended relation qualifies.

Keep evidence of the relationship and purpose. For regular support, a short written explanation plus bank and transfer records can be useful. If the recipient uses the money to earn interest or other income, that later income may have its own tax treatment.
Gifts from relatives

India's Income Tax Department explains that Section 56(2)(x) addresses money or property received without consideration. It also sets out exceptions, including receipts from specified relatives and certain other circumstances.

The department's guidance on deemed income and gifts should be read for the current framework. Because definitions and circumstances matter, a family label alone should not replace professional advice for a large gift.

If a transfer is truly a gift, keep a record stating that it is voluntary, no repayment is expected and the donor has the financial capacity to make it. A formal deed is not a magic solution, but clear documents can help establish the facts.
Also retain source-of-funds evidence. A tax exemption for the recipient does not prevent a bank or provider from checking where a large amount came from.
Gifts from others

Money received without consideration from someone who is not a specified relative may fall within the Indian deemed-income rules when the applicable aggregate threshold is crossed. Official guidance describes an INR 50,000 aggregate test and explains that, where it applies, the whole relevant aggregate can be chargeable rather than only the excess.
This is not a reason to split a gift into smaller transfers. The test is not simply applied one payment at a time, and artificial splitting can make the records less credible.

Exceptions can apply in particular situations, including receipts connected with marriage, inheritance or a will. Each exception has conditions. Confirm the latest rule and the recipient's facts instead of relying on a social-media summary.
If the money is consideration for work, goods, rent or another service, it is not genuinely a no-consideration gift. It should be recorded according to its real commercial character.
Income stays income

Payment from a UK customer to a person in India for work can be income even if it arrives through a consumer transfer service. Salary, consultancy fees, business receipts, rent, interest and sale profits each have their own rules.

The payment description, invoice and contract should agree. Keep records of the gross amount, provider fees, exchange rate and INR credited. A fee deducted before arrival does not necessarily change the gross-income reporting requirement.

Businesses and self-employed recipients should use an appropriate business payment route where required. Consumer remittance services may restrict commercial payments, and using an unsuitable route can create compliance and reconciliation problems.
Ask an Indian tax professional about income recognition, deductions, GST or withholding where relevant. This article cannot determine those obligations from the transfer alone.
Loans and repayments

A genuine repayment of money previously lent is different from a gift, but the parties should be able to show the original loan and repayment terms. Without records, a later credit can be difficult to explain.

If the transfer is a new loan, document the amount, parties, purpose, repayment schedule and any interest. Cross-border lending can involve rules beyond ordinary remittance processing, so obtain advice before using a casual personal-transfer route.
Loan interest can have a separate tax treatment from principal. Do not label an amount "loan repayment" when no genuine loan existed.
Inheritance and estates
An inheritance is not the same as a lifetime gift. Keep the will, probate or succession documents, estate statements and proof of distribution.

The recipient may need to establish why the money was received and whether income or gains arose before distribution. The sender or executor may also have duties in the country administering the estate.

Because UK inheritance-tax and Indian tax questions can interact with residence, domicile, asset location and estate structure, seek specialist advice for material amounts. A provider completing the payment does not confirm that estate reporting is complete.
The UK side
Sending money from a UK bank account does not by itself create a blanket UK remittance tax. The source of the money and the sender's circumstances remain relevant.

If a UK resident earned income or realised a gain, the normal UK rules can apply before the money is sent. Gifts can also be relevant to inheritance-tax planning, particularly where the donor dies within an applicable period or retains a benefit. Those questions are separate from the Indian recipient's position.
Residence rules changed from 6 April 2025 for some foreign income and gains. Do not apply an old "non-domiciled" explanation to a current transfer without checking up-to-date HMRC guidance.

The UK-India double taxation agreement can matter where the same income is taxable in both places, but it does not turn every family remittance into taxable income. Treaty claims depend on the particular income and residence facts.
Transfer charges
Tax is different from transfer cost. A provider's fee, exchange-rate margin, card charge, correspondent deduction or receiving-bank charge is not automatically a tax.

Suppose a sender pays GBP 1,000 and the recipient receives the INR equivalent of GBP 975 after all pricing effects. The GBP 25 difference might contain provider costs or rate margin. It does not by itself tell you the amount reportable for tax.
Use the transfer-fees guide to identify commercial charges. The pound to INR converter offers a reference calculation for comparison, not a tax valuation or provider quote.
Keep the transfer receipt showing the original amount, fees, rate and payout. A clean record is more useful than trying to reconstruct the transaction from a bank balance months later.
Large transfers
There is no contradiction between a tax-free receipt and a compliance review. A provider can ask for identity, source and purpose evidence even where the customer believes no tax is payable.
The documents guide explains common evidence. For a large payment, prepare statements and supporting records before initiating the transfer.
Check the provider's limit and route as well. The UK-to-India transfer limit guide explains why a provider maximum is not a tax exemption or regulatory approval.
Never divide transfers to conceal their total or avoid checks. Related transactions may be reviewed together.
Records to keep
Keep the sender and recipient names, relationship evidence, purpose note, source-of-funds documents, transfer reference, fee statement, exchange rate and bank records on both sides.

For a gift, record that no repayment is expected. For a loan, keep the agreement and repayments. For income, keep invoices and contracts. For inheritance, keep estate documents. For your own-account transfer, keep statements connecting ownership and source.
Store personal information securely. Upload documents only through a verified provider or bank channel, and share no more than requested.
Ask how long records should be retained for the relevant tax filing and transaction type. Different obligations can apply to individuals, businesses, trusts and estates.
Before sending
Write down the true purpose and confirm the recipient account. Check whether the payment is your own money, support, gift, loan, income, purchase or estate distribution.
Confirm whether the recipient is a specified relative if relying on a gift exception. Check any applicable aggregate threshold and special exception with current official guidance.
Review the UK source of funds and any separate income, gains or inheritance issue. For a material or unusual transfer, obtain advice in the relevant country before the money moves.
Finally, compare providers for cost and speed without allowing a cheap quote to distract from correct records and tax treatment.
Common questions
Is money sent to my parents in India taxable?
Gifts from specified relatives can fall within an Indian exception, but confirm the definition, purpose and full circumstances. Keep relationship and transfer records.
Is transferring money to my own Indian account taxable?
The transfer itself does not automatically create new income, but the source of funds, account type, residence and any income or gain still matter.
Is every gift below INR 50,000 tax-free?
Do not treat the threshold as a simple per-transfer allowance. Official guidance describes an aggregate test, and the source and exceptions must be considered.
Are provider fees a tax?
No. Commercial charges and exchange-rate margins are separate from tax, although records may need to show gross amounts and deductions.
Does provider approval prove that no tax is due?
No. A provider decides whether it can process the transfer. Tax treatment is a separate question based on the parties and the underlying transaction.
